outputs.L1:
Children picking up our bones  
Will never know that these were once  
As quick as foxes on the hill,  
Nor that, in autumn, when the grapes  
Made sharp air sharper with their smell,  
These had a being, breathing frost.  

And least of all will they guess that, with our bones,  
We left much more: left what still is—  
The look of things; left what we felt  
At what we saw. The spring clouds blow  
Above the shuttered mansion-house;  
Beyond our gate, the windy sky  
Cries out a literate despair.  

We knew for long the mansion’s look,  
And what we said of it became  
A part of what it is... Children,  
Still weaving budded aureoles,  
Will speak our speech and never know;  
Will say of the mansion that it seems  
As if he who lived there left behind  
A spirit storming through blank walls,  
A dirty house in a gutted world,  
A tatter of shadows peaked to white,  
Smeared with the gold of the opulent sun.
outputs.L2:
When children discover our remains, they will not realize that our bodies were once alive and agile, racing over the hills like foxes. They will not know that, in autumn, we breathed the frosty air while the scent of grapes intensified its sharpness. Even less will they understand that we left behind more than bones: we also passed on our perceptions, our emotions, and the meanings we attached to everything we witnessed.

Spring clouds now drift over the closed-up manor. Outside the gate, the wind-filled sky seems to voice an articulate grief. We studied the house for so long that our descriptions of it eventually became part of its identity. Future children, still making garlands from budding branches, will repeat our words without knowing their source. They will describe the mansion as though its former resident abandoned a restless presence inside its empty walls: a stained dwelling in a ruined world, a pale, ragged mass of shadows streaked by the wealthy sunlight’s gold.
outputs.L3:
Future generations may one day discover the speakers’ bones, yet those remains will reveal little about the vitality, emotions, and sensations they once possessed. Death leaves behind more than physical traces: it also creates an absence where individual perceptions, feelings, and ways of understanding the world once existed. Although these inner experiences cannot be recovered directly, they survive indirectly through language.

The long-abandoned mansion, for example, becomes inseparable from the meanings and descriptions the speakers have attached to it. Its identity is shaped not only by its physical decay but also by the words used to interpret its emptiness, history, and fading magnificence. In time, children will inherit these descriptions and ways of seeing without realizing where they originated. The speakers’ language will pass into collective memory, even as their individual lives are forgotten.

Thus, the mansion endures as more than a ruined building. It becomes a haunting symbol of spiritual desolation, decay, and faded grandeur—a lasting image through which the vanished perceptions of the dead continue to influence the living.
outputs.L4:
The poem reflects on mortality, memory, and inheritance by imagining a future in which children discover the bones of people who have long since died. To those children, the remains will be anonymous: they will not know the names, personalities, experiences, or relationships of the dead. Human lives that once felt immediate and vivid will have been reduced to physical traces. This image emphasizes both the inevitability of death and the fragility of personal memory, suggesting that even lives filled with feeling may eventually become mysterious to later generations.

Against this future anonymity, the poem presents the speakers’ intense awareness of the world around them. They observe nature closely and perceive the decaying mansion not merely as a ruined building but as a place charged with history, emotion, and imaginative significance. The contrast between living perception and lifeless remains is central to the poem. Bones may survive after identity has disappeared, while buildings and landscapes may endure after their original inhabitants are forgotten. Yet these physical remains do not possess a fixed meaning on their own. They become meaningful through the attention, language, and imagination of those who encounter them.

The poem therefore offers a broader understanding of inheritance. Descendants may not remember the dead as individuals, but they inherit the words, ideas, and habits of perception through which earlier generations understood the world. Language allows ways of seeing to pass from one age to another, even when names and biographies have vanished. The future children’s response to the bones, the natural landscape, and the mansion will be shaped by cultural meanings created before they were born.

In this sense, the poem does not present death as complete erasure. Individual identity may fade, but human consciousness continues indirectly through language and interpretation. People leave behind more than their bodies: they leave patterns of thought that influence how later generations imagine the past and understand particular places. The poem ultimately suggests that memory survives not only through factual knowledge of the dead, but also through inherited ways of seeing. By giving meaning to landscapes, ruins, and human remains, language enables the consciousness of one generation to endure within the minds of another.
outputs.L5:
### Children, Will, and the Future

Children are naturally curious, imaginative, and eager to understand the world around them. With encouragement and guidance, they will develop the confidence to explore new ideas, overcome challenges, and express their individuality.

Parents, teachers, and communities share the responsibility of creating safe and supportive environments for children. Education should provide more than knowledge; it should also nurture empathy, creativity, and resilience. When children feel valued and heard, they are more likely to become thoughtful, responsible adults.

The choices we make today will shape their opportunities tomorrow. By investing in children and protecting their rights, we help build a kinder, fairer, and more hopeful future for everyone.
